topics.name: Jupiter
topics.kicker: Largest planet in the solar system · Home of the Great Red Spot
topics.dates: Known since ancient times; Galilean moons found 1610
topics.briefing: Jupiter is so huge that all the other planets could fit inside it, and it has more than twice as much mass as all of them put together. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that astronomers have watched for more than 150 years. In 1610, Galileo spotted four moons circling it, the first proof that not everything in the sky goes around Earth.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1676, Ole Rømer [“ROH-mer”] noticed that eclipses of one of this planet’s moons came earlier or later than expected depending on how far Earth was from this planet, showing that light travels at a finite speed. That moon, Io [“EYE-oh”], is the most volcanically active body in the solar system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this largest planet in the solar system, home of the Great Red Spot.

tossups.p: Three moons of this planet are locked in a 1:2:4 pattern called the Laplace resonance: the innermost circles four times for each orbit of the outermost. The resulting tidal squeezing heats the innermost moon, Io, and may keep an ocean liquid beneath the ice of Europa.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet whose four largest moons were discovered by Galileo in 1610.

tossups.p: While studying Voyager 1 images in 1979, navigation engineer Linda Morabito spotted a plume rising from one of this planet’s moons, the first active volcano ever found beyond Earth. Voyager 1 also discovered this planet’s faint, dusty rings that same year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fifth planet from the Sun, the largest planet in the solar system.

tossups.p: In _Sidereus Nuncius_, or _The Starry Messenger_, a scientist called four objects circling this planet the “Medicean Stars” to honor his patrons, the Medici family. Those objects, first spotted in January 1610, proved that not everything in the sky revolves around Earth.
tossups.r: That scientist was Galileo. For 10 points, name this planet, named for the king of the Roman gods.

tossups.p: This planet gives off more heat than it receives from the Sun, because it is still slowly shrinking and releasing energy, a process called the Kelvin–Helmholtz mechanism. Deep inside it, crushing pressure turns hydrogen into a liquid metal that produces the strongest magnetic field of any planet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas giant with a huge storm called the Great Red Spot.

tossups.p: Between 1998 and 2000, three white storms on this planet merged into a single storm called Oval BA, which later turned red and was nicknamed “Red Spot Junior.” Its larger cousin is a high-pressure storm that has been shrinking but was still wider than Earth in 2025.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet whose Great Red Spot astronomers have watched for more than 150 years.

tossups.p: Daniel Kirkwood explained the gaps in the asteroid belt: an asteroid in one of them would circle the Sun, for example, exactly three times for each orbit of this planet, so this planet’s repeated tugs would pull it away. Thousands of Trojan asteroids share this planet’s orbit at two Lagrange points.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet just beyond the asteroid belt, the largest in the solar system.

tossups.p: Pioneer 10 made the first flyby of this planet in 1973, and the Galileo spacecraft later orbited it for nearly eight years before plunging into its clouds in 2003. In 1995, Galileo had dropped a probe that parachuted into this planet’s atmosphere.
tossups.r: This planet has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined. For 10 points, name this largest planet in the solar system.

tossups.p: In July 1994, more than 20 pieces of Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 slammed into this planet, leaving dark scars in its clouds, some about as wide as Earth. This planet’s gravity had torn that comet apart during a close pass two years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas giant, the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest of all.

tossups.p: A NASA probe named for the goddess who could see through the clouds her husband wrapped around himself began orbiting this planet on July 4, 2016. That probe, Juno, found clusters of giant cyclones swirling around this planet’s poles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, named for the Roman king of the gods.

tossups.p: The fourth movement of Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_ is named for this planet, “the Bringer of Jollity,” and its stately middle tune became the hymn “I Vow to Thee, My Country.” The word “jovial” comes from this planet’s link to good cheer in old astrology.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas giant, the largest planet in the solar system and the fifth from the Sun.

tossups.p: This planet’s moon Ganymede [“GAN-ih-meed”] is the only moon known to make its own magnetic field, and it is bigger than the planet Mercury. Another of this planet’s moons, Callisto, is one of the most heavily cratered objects in the solar system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet whose moon Europa may hide an ocean beneath its icy crust.

tossups.p: In 2023, Europe launched a mission called JUICE to study this planet’s icy moons, and in 2024 NASA launched Europa Clipper to learn whether one of them could support life. That moon is thought to hide a salty ocean of liquid water beneath its frozen crust.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose moon Europa was discovered by Galileo along with Io, Ganymede, and Callisto.

tossups.p: Because it spins once in just under 10 hours, the fastest rotation of any planet, this planet bulges noticeably at its equator. Its clouds are stretched into light-colored bands called zones and darker bands called belts.
tossups.r: Its Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth. For 10 points, name this largest planet in the solar system.

tossups.p: Simon Marius, who claimed he had spotted them on his own, gave four of this planet’s moons the names they still carry, all taken from Greek myths. Those four moons were the first objects ever found orbiting a planet other than Earth.
tossups.r: The giant planets are often called “Jovian,” meaning “like this planet.” For 10 points, name this largest planet in the solar system.

Fifth planet from the Sun, the first one beyond the asteroid belt

Named for the king of the Roman gods, the counterpart of the Greek Zeus
Its moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than the planet Mercury, and the only moon known to make its own magnetic field
Its moon Io is the most volcanically active body in the solar system
Its moon Europa is thought to hide a salty ocean of liquid water under an icy crust, making it a top place to look for life
Spins faster than any other planet: a day lasts just under 10 hours, so it bulges at its equator
Its cloud stripes are light-colored zones and darker belts
More than 20 pieces of Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 slammed into it in July 1994
NASA’s Juno probe, named for the wife of its namesake god, began orbiting it on July 4, 2016, and found giant cyclones at its poles
Deep inside, crushing pressure turns hydrogen into a liquid metal that creates the strongest magnetic field of any planet
Gustav Holst’s suite _The Planets_ calls it “the Bringer of Jollity”
The words “jovial” and “Jovian” (used for the giant planets) come from Jove, another name for its namesake god
Ole Rømer timed eclipses of its moon Io to show in 1676 that light travels at a finite speed
Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 orbital pattern called the Laplace resonance
Linda Morabito spotted a volcanic plume on Io in Voyager 1 images (1979), the first active volcano found beyond Earth
Voyager 1 discovered its faint, dusty rings in 1979
Galileo named its four big moons the “Medicean Stars” for the Medici family in _Sidereus Nuncius_ (_The Starry Messenger_)
Simon Marius claimed he found the four big moons on his own and gave them their names from Greek myths
Gives off more heat than it gets from the Sun because it is slowly shrinking (the Kelvin–Helmholtz mechanism)
Oval BA, nicknamed “Red Spot Junior,” formed when three white storms merged between 1998 and 2000
Its repeated tugs clear out the Kirkwood gaps in the asteroid belt
Thousands of Trojan asteroids share its orbit at two Lagrange points; NASA’s Lucy probe, launched in 2021, was sent to visit them
Pioneer 10 made the first flyby (1973); the Galileo orbiter (1995–2003) dropped a probe into its atmosphere
Europe’s JUICE (launched 2023) and NASA’s Europa Clipper (launched 2024) were sent to study its icy moons
Its moon Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered objects in the solar system

trap.title: Moon clue, planet answer
trap.body: Many Jupiter tossups lead with clues about its moons: Io’s volcanoes, Europa’s hidden ocean, Ganymede’s magnetic field. Players who recognize the moon blurt out “Io” or “Europa,” but the question asks for the planet. Saturn, the other gas giant with a huge family of moons, is the next most common wrong answer, and Zeus is only the Greek god, not the planet.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this planet” wants the planet, even if every clue so far was about a moon. Galileo’s four moons, the Great Red Spot, Shoemaker–Levy 9, and the Juno probe mean Jupiter; bright icy rings, Titan, Enceladus, the hexagon, and the Cassini mission mean Saturn.

topics.name: Mars
topics.kicker: Fourth planet from the Sun · The Red Planet, explored by rovers
topics.dates: Known since ancient times; moons found 1877
topics.briefing: Mars looks red because its dusty surface is full of iron oxide, the same stuff as rust. It has the solar system’s largest volcano, Olympus Mons, and a canyon system, Valles Marineris, about as long as the United States is wide. Robots have explored it for decades, from the Viking landers of 1976 to the Perseverance rover and its little helicopter, Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet in 2021.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The largest crater on this planet’s moon Phobos [“FOH-bus”] is named Stickney, after the wife of the astronomer who discovered both of this planet’s moons in 1877. That astronomer, Asaph Hall, was working at the U.S. Naval Observatory.
tossups.r: This planet is named for the Roman god of war. For 10 points, name this fourth planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: In _Gulliver’s Travels_, astronomers on the flying island of Laputa know of two moons circling this planet, more than 150 years before real astronomers found them. Those real moons, Phobos and Deimos [“DYE-mus”], may be asteroids that this planet captured.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rusty-red planet, the fourth from the Sun, named for the Roman god of war.

tossups.p: Johannes Kepler spent years trying to fit Tycho Brahe’s careful measurements of this planet’s position, a struggle that led him to realize that planets move in ellipses. This planet sometimes seems to loop backward across the night sky, which is called retrograde motion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, named for the Roman god of war and nicknamed the Red Planet.

tossups.p: A meteorite called ALH84001, found in Antarctica in 1984, came from this planet, and in 1996 a team of NASA scientists claimed that it might hold tiny fossils of ancient microbes. Many other scientists disputed that claim.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose two small moons are Phobos and Deimos.

tossups.p: Edgar Rice Burroughs called this planet “Barsoom” in adventure novels about John Carter, and Ray Bradbury wrote a 1950 book of linked stories about rocket ships carrying settlers there from Earth.
tossups.r: In H. G. Wells’s _The War of the Worlds_, invaders from this planet attack England. For 10 points, name this fourth planet.

tossups.p: Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite _The Planets_ opens with a pounding movement in 5/4 time that calls this planet “the Bringer of War.” In Roman myth, the god this planet is named for was the father of Romulus and Remus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet whose surface is reddened by iron oxide.

tossups.p: A canyon system on this planet about as long as the United States is wide is named for Mariner 9, which in 1971 became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet. Mariner 4 had sent back the first close-up photos of this planet six years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, home of Valles Marineris and of Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the solar system.

tossups.p: The Tharsis region of this planet holds a line of three huge volcanoes named Arsia, Pavonis, and Ascraeus [“ass-KREE-us”] Mons. Nearby stands the largest volcano in the solar system, a shield volcano about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.
tossups.r: That volcano is Olympus Mons. For 10 points, name this fourth planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: A rover built to last 90 sols, or days on this planet, kept working for more than 14 years, until a planet-wide dust storm blocked its solar power in 2018. That rover, Opportunity, landed in 2004, as did its twin, Spirit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet nicknamed the Red Planet, the fourth from the Sun.

tossups.p: A small helicopter named Ingenuity made 72 flights on this planet, starting with the first powered, controlled flight on another planet in April 2021. It rode to Jezero [“JEZ-uh-roh”] Crater, a dried-up lake bed, attached to the belly of a rover.
tossups.r: That rover is Perseverance. For 10 points, name this planet, which NASA rovers have explored since 1997.

tossups.p: In 2012, a rocket-powered “sky crane” lowered the Curiosity rover on cables into this planet’s Gale Crater, where it later began climbing a mountain called Mount Sharp. Curiosity found evidence that the crater once held a lake.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose polar ice caps contain frozen carbon dioxide, or dry ice.

tossups.p: Giovanni Schiaparelli [“skyah-puh-REL-ee”] described “canali,” or channels, on this planet, a word mistranslated into English as “canals.” Percival Lowell built an observatory in Arizona and wrote books claiming that intelligent beings had dug those canals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, home of the giant volcano Olympus Mons and the canyon Valles Marineris.

tossups.p: In 1976, a photo of the Cydonia [“sih-DOH-nee-uh”] region taken by the Viking 1 orbiter showed a hill that looked like a human face, but sharper photos taken years later showed an ordinary mesa. The Viking landers tested this planet’s soil for signs of life.
tossups.r: Viking 1 also sent back the first clear photos from this planet’s surface. For 10 points, name this planet, named for the Roman god of war.

tossups.p: India’s Mangalyaan orbiter reached this planet in 2014, and China’s Zhurong [“joo-RONG”] rover landed on it in 2021. Both missions studied a world whose thin atmosphere is made mostly of carbon dioxide.
tossups.r: This planet has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. For 10 points, name this fourth planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: A day on this planet, called a sol, lasts about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth, and its axis is tilted about 25 degrees, so it has seasons, though each lasts about twice as long as Earth’s.
tossups.r: A year there lasts about 687 Earth days. For 10 points, name this planet, whose reddish color comes from iron oxide, or rust.

clues.t: Called the Red Planet because iron oxide (rust) in its dust colors its surface
Fourth planet from the Sun, between Earth and the asteroid belt
Named for the Roman god of war, the counterpart of the Greek Ares; the month of March is named for the same god
Home of Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the solar system
Explored by NASA rovers: Sojourner (1997), Spirit and Opportunity (2004), Curiosity (2012), and Perseverance (2021)
Its two small moons, Phobos (“fear”) and Deimos (“dread”), are named for sons of Ares and may be captured asteroids
Valles Marineris, a canyon system about as long as the United States is wide, is named for the Mariner 9 orbiter
Its polar ice caps hold water ice and frozen carbon dioxide (dry ice)
Its thin atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, and dust storms sometimes cover the entire planet
Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater in 2021 carrying Ingenuity, the first helicopter to make a powered, controlled flight on another planet
Curiosity was lowered into Gale Crater in 2012 by a rocket-powered “sky crane” and climbed Mount Sharp
Giovanni Schiaparelli’s “canali” (channels) were mistranslated as “canals,” and Percival Lowell claimed intelligent beings had built them
Invaders from this planet attack England in H. G. Wells’s _The War of the Worlds_ (1898)
A year there lasts about 687 Earth days; a day, called a sol, lasts about 40 minutes longer than Earth’s
Asaph Hall discovered both moons in 1877 at the U.S. Naval Observatory
Stickney, the largest crater on Phobos, is named for Asaph Hall’s wife, Angeline Stickney
Jonathan Swift’s _Gulliver’s Travels_ (1726) gave it two moons more than 150 years before they were found
Johannes Kepler used Tycho Brahe’s measurements of its orbit to discover that planets move in ellipses
Meteorite ALH84001, found in Antarctica in 1984, came from here; in 1996 NASA scientists claimed it held possible microbe fossils
The Viking landers (1976) tested its soil for life; a Viking 1 orbiter photo of a hill in the Cydonia region looked like a face
Mariner 4 sent back the first close-up photos (1965); Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet (1971)
The Tharsis region holds a row of three giant volcanoes: Arsia, Pavonis, and Ascraeus Mons
Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_ opens with its movement, “the Bringer of War,” written in 5/4 time
India’s Mangalyaan orbiter arrived in 2014; China’s Zhurong rover landed in 2021
Opportunity, designed to last 90 sols, worked for more than 14 years, until a planet-wide dust storm in 2018
Edgar Rice Burroughs called it “Barsoom” in his John Carter adventure novels

trap.title: Planet, not its parts
trap.body: Mars tossups are full of famous features that are also answer lines of their own, like Olympus Mons, Phobos, and the Curiosity rover. When a clue names one of them, players sometimes blurt out the feature instead of the planet. The other slip is mythology: Ares is the Greek war god, and only the Roman name, Mars, is the planet.
trap.fix: Listen for “this planet.” Phobos and Deimos, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, and Ingenuity all point to the Red Planet, the fourth from the Sun. Only answer with a feature if the question asks for “this volcano,” “this moon,” or “this rover.”

topics.name: Comets
topics.kicker: Icy wanderers with glowing tails · Visitors from the edge of the solar system
topics.briefing: Comets are “dirty snowballs” of ice, dust, and rock that spend most of their time in the frozen outer solar system. When one swings close to the Sun, its ice turns to gas, puffing up a fuzzy cloud called a coma and long tails that always point away from the Sun. The most famous, Halley’s Comet, returns about every 76 years; it came by in 1986 and is due back in 2061.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: By showing that one of these objects had no measurable parallax in 1577, Tycho Brahe proved it was farther away than the Moon. That disproved Aristotle’s teaching that these objects were glowing vapors high in Earth’s air.
tossups.r: These icy bodies grow a fuzzy coma and long tails as they near the Sun. For 10 points, name these “dirty snowballs.”

tossups.p: Charles Messier [“MESS-ee-ay”] listed more than 100 fuzzy objects, such as nebulae and star clusters, so that he would not confuse them with these objects, which he spent his career hunting. The name of these objects comes from a Greek word meaning “long-haired.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies whose glowing tails point away from the Sun.

tossups.p: Fred Whipple’s 1950 “icy conglomerate” model explained that each of these objects has a solid nucleus of frozen gases mixed with dust. When one of these bodies nears the Sun, its ice sublimates, turning straight into gas that forms a fuzzy cloud called a coma.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these “dirty snowballs,” the most famous of which returns about every 76 years.

tossups.p: Some of these objects seem to grow an “antitail” that points toward the Sun, which is really a trick of perspective. Each of these objects usually has a curved, yellowish dust tail and a straight, bluish ion tail pushed outward by the solar wind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies whose tails always point away from the Sun.

tossups.p: A European probe named for the painter Giotto [“JOT-oh”], who may have painted one of these objects as the Star of Bethlehem, flew past the most famous of them in 1986. That same object, seen in 1066, months before the Battle of Hastings, appears on the Bayeux Tapestry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies with glowing tails, including one named for Edmond Halley.

tossups.p: In 2014, a lander named Philae bounced across the surface of 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko [“choo-RYOO-mof geh-rah-sih-MEN-koh”], becoming the first spacecraft to land on one of these objects. Its mother ship, Rosetta, was named for the stone that helped scholars decode Egyptian hieroglyphs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies that form a coma and tails near the Sun.

tossups.p: On July 4, 2005, NASA’s Deep Impact mission fired a copper impactor into Tempel 1, one of these objects, to blast out material from beneath its surface. Another NASA mission, Stardust, brought dust from one of these objects back to Earth in 2006.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies that develop long tails when they near the Sun.

tossups.p: Amateur astronomer Gennady Borisov discovered the first known one of these objects to come from another star system, in 2019. Most of these objects come from two distant reservoirs: the Kuiper Belt and the much farther Oort cloud.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies, nicknamed “dirty snowballs,” that grow tails as they near the Sun.

tossups.p: Using Isaac Newton’s laws, an English astronomer showed that the bright objects seen in 1531, 1607, and 1682 were the same one of these bodies, and he predicted its return in 1758. It came back as predicted, years after his death, and was later given the designation 1P.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies, whose most famous example is named for Edmond Halley.

tossups.p: Mark Twain was born in 1835, when one of these objects was visible, and he said he expected to die when it came back. He did, in 1910, one day after it passed closest to the Sun.
tossups.r: That object, named for Edmond Halley, returns about every 76 years. For 10 points, name these icy bodies with glowing tails.

tossups.p: Dust shed by one of these objects causes both the Orionid meteor shower in October and the Eta Aquariid [“AY-tuh uh-KWAIR-ee-id”] shower in May. The Perseid shower each August comes from the debris of another one, Swift–Tuttle, which returns about every 133 years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these “dirty snowballs” whose leftover dust causes many meteor showers.

tossups.p: Discovered separately by Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp in 1995, one of these objects stayed visible to the naked eye for about a year and a half, a record. Its coma and two tails glowed brightly in the night sky during 1997.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies, which come from the Kuiper Belt and the Oort cloud.

tossups.p: Ernst Öpik [“UH-pik”] and Jan Oort proposed that a vast, round cloud of icy bodies at the far edge of the solar system sends these objects falling toward the Sun on orbits that can take thousands of years. Shorter-period ones often come from the Kuiper Belt instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these “dirty snowballs,” such as Hale–Bopp and the one named for Edmond Halley.

tossups.p: In 1992, Jupiter’s gravity tore one of these objects into more than 20 pieces, which smashed into Jupiter two years later. That object, Shoemaker–Levy 9, was named for the three astronomers who discovered it in 1993.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these icy bodies that form a coma and a tail when they come near the Sun.

tossups.p: In 2013, a sungrazing one of these objects named ISON fell apart as it swung close to the Sun. Most of these objects spend nearly all their time far out in the frozen outer solar system, where they are too cold to grow tails.
tossups.r: When they near the Sun, they grow a fuzzy coma and tails that point away from it. For 10 points, name these icy bodies, nicknamed “dirty snowballs.”

clues.t: Icy bodies nicknamed “dirty snowballs,” made of ice, dust, and rock
Near the Sun they grow glowing tails that always point away from the Sun
The most famous, named for Edmond Halley, returns about every 76 years (it came by in 1986 and is due back in 2061)
The solid center is the nucleus; near the Sun it puffs up a fuzzy cloud of gas and dust called the coma
Long-period ones come from the distant Oort cloud; many short-period ones come from the Kuiper Belt
Usually two tails: a curved, yellowish dust tail and a straight, bluish ion tail pushed by the solar wind
Near the Sun their ice sublimates, turning straight from solid to gas
Earth passing through their leftover dust causes meteor showers, like the Perseids from Swift–Tuttle
Fred Whipple proposed the “dirty snowball” (icy conglomerate) model in 1950
Edmond Halley used Newton’s laws to show the visitors of 1531, 1607, and 1682 were one object, and predicted its return in 1758
Mark Twain was born in 1835 and died in 1910, both years when the one named for Halley passed close to the Sun
Shoemaker–Levy 9 was torn apart by Jupiter’s gravity and crashed into Jupiter in 1994
The one named for Halley appears on the Bayeux Tapestry, which shows it in the sky in 1066 before the Battle of Hastings
Their name comes from a Greek word meaning “long-haired”
Tycho Brahe found no parallax for the bright one of 1577, proving it lay beyond the Moon, not in Earth’s air as Aristotle had taught
Charles Messier hunted them and cataloged fuzzy look-alikes such as nebulae so he would not be fooled, creating the Messier catalog
ESA’s Rosetta orbited 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko, and its lander Philae made the first landing on one, in 2014
NASA’s Deep Impact fired a copper impactor into Tempel 1 on July 4, 2005
NASA’s Stardust caught dust from Wild 2 [“VILT”] in a spongy material called aerogel and returned it to Earth in 2006
ESA’s Giotto probe flew past the one named for Halley in 1986; it was named for the painter who probably showed that same object as the Star of Bethlehem
Ernst Öpik (1932) and Jan Oort (1950) proposed a vast, round cloud of icy bodies at the solar system’s edge
An “antitail” seems to point toward the Sun, but it is just a trick of perspective
2I/Borisov, found in 2019 by amateur astronomer Gennady Borisov, was the first known interstellar one
The one named for Halley was the first recognized as periodic, so it is designated 1P
Hale–Bopp (found in 1995, brightest in 1997) stayed visible to the naked eye for a record of about 18 months
Dust from the one named for Halley causes the Orionid (October) and Eta Aquariid (May) meteor showers
The sungrazer ISON broke apart near the Sun in 2013

trap.title: Comet, asteroid, or meteor?
trap.body: Comets get mixed up with rocky asteroids and with meteors, the streaks of light made when bits of space dust burn up in Earth’s air. Players also hear “Edmond Halley” and blurt out “Halley’s Comet” when the question wants the whole group. And the Oort cloud and the Kuiper Belt are where comets come from, not the objects themselves.
trap.fix: A coma, a tail, ice that sublimates, or the nickname “dirty snowball” means comets. Rocky bodies in the belt between Mars and Jupiter are asteroids; a streak of light in the sky is a meteor; a space rock that reaches the ground is a meteorite. If the question says “these objects,” give the general term, not one famous example.

topics.name: Neptune
topics.kicker: Eighth and farthest planet · The first planet found by math
topics.briefing: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun, so far away that it was found with math before anyone knew where to look. In 1846, astronomers used tugs on Uranus’s orbit to predict where an unseen planet should be, and Johann Galle spotted it the very night he received the prediction. This blue ice giant has the fastest winds of any planet, and as of 2025 only one spacecraft, Voyager 2, had ever visited it.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The outermost ring of this planet is clumped into bright arcs named Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité, and Courage. That ring is named for John Couch Adams, one of two mathematicians who separately predicted where this planet would be found.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this eighth planet from the Sun, discovered in 1846.

tossups.p: Just 17 days after this planet was discovered, William Lassell found its largest moon, which orbits in the opposite direction from the planet’s spin. That moon, Triton, is probably an object captured from the Kuiper Belt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this blue ice giant, the farthest planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: James Challis of Cambridge recorded this planet twice in the summer of 1846 without realizing what it was. Weeks later, Johann Galle [“GAH-luh”] found it at the Berlin Observatory, very close to where Urbain Le Verrier [“luh-vair-YAY”] had predicted it would be.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ice giant, the eighth and farthest planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: Galileo sketched this planet in his notebooks in 1612 and 1613, but he thought it was just a faint star. It was finally recognized as a planet in 1846, after Le Verrier [“luh-vair-YAY”] used the tugs it caused on Uranus to calculate its position.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this eighth planet, named for the Roman god of the sea.

tossups.p: Gerard Kuiper [“KY-per”] discovered this planet’s moon Nereid [“NEER-ee-id”] in 1949, and Nereid’s orbit is one of the most stretched-out of any moon in the solar system. In 1989, Voyager 2 found this planet’s second-largest moon, a dark, lumpy body named Proteus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet whose largest moon, Triton, orbits backward around it.

tossups.p: Voyager 2 photographed a fast-moving white cloud on this planet nicknamed “the Scooter,” as well as a giant storm called the Great Dark Spot. When the Hubble Space Telescope looked in 1994, that storm had vanished.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this blue ice giant, the eighth planet from the Sun, which Voyager 2 flew past in 1989.

tossups.p: This planet gives off far more heat than it receives from the Sun, unlike Uranus, which is slightly larger but less massive. Methane in this planet’s atmosphere absorbs red light, which helps give this planet its blue color.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ice giant, the farthest planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: From 1979 to 1999, this planet was farther from the Sun than Pluto, because Pluto’s stretched-out orbit had carried it inside this planet’s path. The two never collide because Pluto orbits twice for every three orbits of this planet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this eighth planet, named for the Roman sea god.

tossups.p: Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_ ends with a movement called “the Mystic,” named for this planet, in which an offstage choir of women’s voices slowly fades into silence. Element 93 is named for this planet.
tossups.r: Its astronomical symbol is a trident. For 10 points, name this eighth planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: Scientists think the crushing pressure deep inside this planet may squeeze carbon into diamonds that sink like hail. This planet and Uranus are called ice giants because they contain lots of water, ammonia, and methane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this blue planet, the eighth from the Sun, whose largest moon is Triton.

tossups.p: Voyager 2 spotted geysers shooting nitrogen gas from the frozen surface of this planet’s largest moon, one of the coldest places ever measured in the solar system. That moon, Triton, orbits this planet backward.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this farthest planet from the Sun, named for the Roman god of the sea.

tossups.p: In 2011, this planet completed its first full trip around the Sun since its discovery, an orbit that takes about 165 Earth years. Because its axis is tilted, each of its seasons lasts about 40 years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet that Johann Galle discovered in 1846, using predictions by Urbain Le Verrier.

tossups.p: Urbain Le Verrier [“luh-vair-YAY”] in France and John Couch Adams in England separately used small tugs on Uranus’s orbit to predict where this planet must be. It became the first planet discovered through mathematical prediction rather than by searching the sky.
tossups.r: Johann Galle spotted it on his first night of searching. For 10 points, name this eighth planet.

tossups.p: This planet has the fastest winds of any planet in the solar system, topping 1,000 miles per hour. Voyager 2 tracked giant storms there when it flew past in 1989, including one about as wide as Earth.
tossups.r: Its largest moon is Triton. For 10 points, name this ice giant, the eighth planet from the Sun.

tossups.p: In August 1989, Voyager 2 made its last planetary flyby at this planet, passing close above its north pole before swinging toward its largest moon. That moon has a pinkish surface streaked with dark material from geysers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet whose moon Triton was discovered just weeks after the planet itself.

clues.t: The eighth and farthest planet from the Sun (since Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006)
Named for the Roman god of the sea, the counterpart of the Greek Poseidon; its symbol is a trident
The first planet found by mathematical prediction, from the tugs it caused on Uranus’s orbit
As of 2025, Voyager 2 (which flew past in 1989) was the only spacecraft to have visited it
A blue ice giant; methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light
Urbain Le Verrier (France) and John Couch Adams (England) separately calculated where it should be
Johann Galle found it at the Berlin Observatory on September 23, 1846, close to the spot Le Verrier predicted
Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backward (retrograde) and is probably a captured Kuiper Belt object
Voyager 2 saw a giant storm, the Great Dark Spot, in 1989; it was gone when the Hubble Space Telescope looked in 1994
Has the fastest winds of any planet, topping 1,000 miles per hour
Pluto orbits the Sun twice for every three of its orbits, so the two never collide
Galileo saw it in 1612 and 1613 but thought it was a star
One orbit takes about 165 Earth years; it finished its first orbit since its discovery in 2011
Element 93 is named for it, just as element 92 is named for the planet just inside its orbit
William Lassell discovered Triton just 17 days after the planet itself was found
Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers on Triton, one of the coldest surfaces measured in the solar system
Its outermost ring, the Adams ring, has bright arcs named Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité, and Courage
James Challis of Cambridge recorded it twice in 1846 without realizing it was a planet
Gerard Kuiper discovered its moon Nereid in 1949; Nereid has one of the most stretched-out orbits of any moon
Its second-largest moon, the dark, lumpy Proteus, was found in Voyager 2 images in 1989
Unlike Uranus, it gives off far more heat than it receives from the Sun
Slightly smaller than Uranus, but more massive and denser
Voyager 2 also tracked a fast-moving white cloud nicknamed “the Scooter”
From 1979 to 1999, it was the farthest planet from the Sun, because Pluto had moved inside its orbit
Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_ ends with its movement, “the Mystic,” which fades out with an offstage choir of women’s voices
Scientists think high pressure deep inside may squeeze carbon into diamonds that sink like hail
Its tilted axis gives it seasons that each last about 40 years

trap.title: Neptune or Uranus?
trap.body: Uranus and Neptune are look-alike blue ice giants, and Neptune was only found because of Uranus: Le Verrier and Adams used tugs on Uranus’s orbit to predict where Neptune was. Players who hear “Uranus” early in a clue sometimes blurt it out. Mythology is the other trap: Poseidon is the Greek sea god, and only the Roman name is the planet.
trap.fix: Le Verrier, Adams, Galle, 1846, Triton, the Great Dark Spot, and the fastest winds mean Neptune. William Herschel, 1781, a sideways tilt, and moons named mostly for Shakespeare characters mean Uranus.

topics.name: Dark matter
topics.kicker: Invisible mass that holds galaxies together · Detected only by its gravity
topics.briefing: Most of the matter in the universe is invisible dark matter: it gives off no light, yet its gravity holds galaxies and galaxy clusters together. In 1933 Fritz Zwicky noticed that galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast to be held by their stars alone, and in the 1970s Vera Rubin showed that stars at the edges of galaxies orbit surprisingly fast. As of 2025, what it is actually made of remained one of science’s biggest mysteries.
topics.answerHtml: Dark matter (accept cold dark matter; do not accept “dark energy”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1933, Fritz Zwicky [“TSVIK-ee”] applied the virial theorem to the Coma Cluster and found that its galaxies were moving far too fast to be held together by the gravity of their visible stars alone. He concluded that the cluster must contain huge amounts of unseen mass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible substance that makes up most of the matter in the universe and is detected only by its gravity.

tossups.p: Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast stars and gas clouds orbit in the Andromeda Galaxy and found that those far from its center move about as fast as those near it. Those flat rotation curves suggested that galaxies are wrapped in halos of unseen mass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible form of matter that gives off no light but has gravity.

tossups.p: When two galaxy clusters smashed together to form the Bullet Cluster, X-ray telescopes showed their hot gas piling up in the middle, but gravitational lensing showed that most of their mass had passed right through. That 2006 result was hailed as direct evidence for this substance.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mysterious, invisible matter that neither gives off nor absorbs light but still has gravity.

tossups.p: Frank Wilczek [“WIL-chek”] named a hypothetical particle after a brand of laundry detergent, and that particle, the axion, is one proposed explanation for this substance. Another candidate is a class of weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible matter that holds galaxies together with its gravity.

tossups.p: Mordehai Milgrom’s theory called MOND, short for Modified Newtonian Dynamics, tries to explain why galaxies spin so fast without needing this substance, by changing the law of gravity instead. Most astronomers favor this substance as the explanation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible matter, first proposed by Fritz Zwicky after he studied the Coma Cluster.

tossups.p: Deep in a former gold mine in South Dakota, the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment uses tons of liquid xenon to try to catch a rare collision between an atom and a particle of this substance. Such underground experiments are shielded from cosmic rays by thousands of feet of rock.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this unseen substance that makes up most of the matter in the universe.

tossups.p: Surveys that watched for stars briefly brightening by gravitational lensing tested whether this substance is made of MACHOs, or massive compact halo objects, such as brown dwarfs. Those surveys found too few MACHOs to explain most of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible material whose gravity holds galaxies and galaxy clusters together.

tossups.p: Some supersymmetry theories predict a stable particle called the neutralino, which could make up this substance. Because this substance is thought to be mostly “cold,” or slow-moving, the standard model of cosmology is called Lambda-CDM.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mysterious, invisible substance that makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe.

tossups.p: Tiny ripples in the cosmic microwave background measured by the WMAP and Planck spacecraft revealed that this substance outweighs ordinary matter by about five to one. Its gravity helped pull ordinary gas together into the first galaxies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible matter, whose existence was first suggested by Fritz Zwicky.

tossups.p: Neutrinos were once proposed as a “hot,” fast-moving form of this substance, but they are too light and too fast to explain how galaxies formed. This substance does not interact with light at all, so no telescope can see it directly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this substance, detected only through its gravity, that Vera Rubin found evidence for in spinning galaxies.

tossups.p: In 2023, Europe launched the Euclid space telescope to map where this substance lies across billions of light-years, by measuring how its gravity slightly warps the shapes of distant galaxies. Astronomers think most galaxies sit inside a huge halo of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible matter that gives off no light but makes up most of the mass of galaxies.

tossups.p: A large observatory in Chile is named for the astronomer whose studies of spinning galaxies provided key evidence for this substance. That astronomer, Vera Rubin, found that stars at the outer edges of spiral galaxies orbit surprisingly fast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible form of matter, which makes up most of the matter in the universe.

tossups.p: Some scientists have suggested that this substance could be made of primordial black holes formed in the first moments after the Big Bang, while others have searched for its particles in collisions at the Large Hadron Collider.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this invisible matter, which, unlike ordinary matter, gives off no light.

tossups.p: The Milky Way’s visible disk of stars sits inside a much larger, roughly round cloud, or halo, made mostly of this substance. This substance can be mapped by gravitational lensing, because its gravity bends light from more distant galaxies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mysterious, invisible substance that gives off no light.

tossups.p: Astronomers estimate that about 5 percent of the universe’s mass and energy is ordinary matter, about 68 percent is a mysterious energy that speeds up its expansion, and about 27 percent is this substance.
tossups.r: Its gravity holds galaxies and galaxy clusters together. For 10 points, name this invisible substance that gives off no light.

clues.t: Invisible matter that gives off no light; it is detected only through its gravity
Makes up most of the matter in the universe, about 85 percent
Fritz Zwicky proposed it in 1933 after galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast
In the 1970s, Vera Rubin and Kent Ford found that stars far from galaxies’ centers orbit surprisingly fast
Its extra gravity holds galaxies and galaxy clusters together
Galaxies’ “flat rotation curves” (outer stars orbiting about as fast as inner ones) are a key sign of it
Most galaxies, including the Milky Way, sit inside a huge, roughly round halo of it
Astronomers map it with gravitational lensing, since its gravity bends light from more distant galaxies
In the Bullet Cluster (2006), lensing showed that most of two colliding clusters’ mass had moved apart from their X-ray-glowing hot gas
A leading candidate: WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles
MACHOs (massive compact halo objects) such as brown dwarfs were tested, but there are too few of them to explain it
The standard Lambda-CDM model of cosmology says most of it is “cold,” or slow-moving
Europe’s Euclid space telescope (launched 2023) maps it by how its gravity warps the shapes of distant galaxies
Neutrinos are a “hot,” fast-moving form of it, but they are too light and fast to be most of it
Zwicky used the virial theorem, which links the motions inside a cluster to its total mass
Rubin and Ford’s famous early study measured how fast stars and gas clouds orbit in the Andromeda Galaxy
Another candidate, the axion, was named by Frank Wilczek after a laundry detergent
Mordehai Milgrom’s MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) tries to explain fast-spinning galaxies by changing gravity instead
Underground detectors filled with liquid xenon, like LUX-ZEPLIN in a former South Dakota gold mine, hunt for its particles
The cosmic microwave background, measured by WMAP and Planck, shows it outweighs ordinary matter about five to one
Some supersymmetry theories predict a WIMP called the neutralino
The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile honors the astronomer whose spinning-galaxy studies supported it
Physicists have searched for its particles in collisions at the Large Hadron Collider
Primordial black holes from the first moments after the Big Bang are another proposed candidate
Its gravity helped pull gas together into the first galaxies
Of the universe’s mass and energy, about 5 percent is ordinary matter, about 68 percent is a mysterious energy that speeds up expansion, and about 27 percent is this

trap.title: Matter, not energy
trap.body: Dark matter and dark energy sound alike but do opposite jobs: dark matter’s gravity pulls galaxies together, while dark energy speeds up the expansion of the whole universe. Answering “dark energy” is wrong. Antimatter is a third mix-up: it is made of particles like positrons, which physicists can make in laboratories.
trap.fix: Zwicky, Vera Rubin, rotation curves, halos, lensing, the Bullet Cluster, WIMPs, and axions mean dark matter. Type Ia supernovae, the speeding-up of the universe’s expansion, and the cosmological constant mean dark energy.
trap.line: Real answer line: Dark matter (accept cold dark matter; do not accept “dark energy”)

topics.name: Neutron stars
topics.kicker: Collapsed cores of massive stars · More mass than the Sun in a city-sized ball
topics.briefing: When a very massive star explodes as a supernova, its core can collapse into a neutron star: a ball only about 20 kilometers (12 miles) across that holds more mass than the Sun. A teaspoon of its material would weigh billions of tons. Some neutron stars spin rapidly, up to hundreds of times a second, and sweep beams of radio waves across space like a lighthouse; astronomers call those pulsars.
topics.answerHtml: Neutron stars (accept neutron star; prompt on stars; do not accept “pulsars” or “magnetars”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Physicists think the crusts of these objects may contain “nuclear pasta,” matter squeezed into shapes nicknamed gnocchi, spaghetti, and lasagna. Deeper inside, these objects may hold a superfluid, which could explain sudden speedups in their spin called glitches.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these super-dense remnants of supernovae, some of which are seen as pulsars.

tossups.p: Scorpius X-1, the first X-ray source found beyond the solar system, is one of these objects pulling gas off a companion star. In 1932, James Chadwick discovered the particle that makes up most of these objects.
tossups.r: These objects, about 20 kilometers across, hold more mass than the Sun. For 10 points, name these collapsed stellar cores.

tossups.p: Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor won a Nobel Prize for finding a pair of these objects orbiting each other, whose slowly shrinking orbit matched Albert Einstein’s prediction of gravitational waves. One of that pair is a pulsar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these extremely dense stellar remnants, denser than white dwarfs but not quite black holes.

tossups.p: The first planets confirmed outside the solar system, found in 1992 by Aleksander Wolszczan [“VOHL-shchahn”] and Dale Frail, orbit one of these objects. That object is a pulsar that spins about 160 times every second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these tiny, super-dense stars left behind when massive stars explode as supernovae.

tossups.p: In August 2017, LIGO and Virgo detected gravitational waves from two of these objects spiraling together, and telescopes then spotted the collision’s glow, called a kilonova. Astronomers found that such crashes forge gold, platinum, and other heavy elements.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these city-sized stellar remnants, some of which are pulsars.

tossups.p: NASA mounted an X-ray instrument called NICER on the International Space Station in 2017 to measure the sizes of these objects and learn what fills their cores. Only about 20 kilometers across, these objects can hold up to about twice the mass of the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these collapsed stars, so dense that a teaspoon of their material would weigh billions of tons.

tossups.p: In 1968, Thomas Gold argued that pulsars are spinning examples of these objects, and that year astronomers found one spinning about 30 times a second inside the Crab Nebula. That nebula is the wreck of a star that Chinese astronomers saw explode in 1054 CE.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these super-dense remnants left after supernovae, each only about the size of a city.

tossups.p: Some of these objects are called “recycled” because gas pulled from a companion star has spun them up until they turn hundreds of times every second. Those millisecond pulsars keep time so steadily that astronomers use them like cosmic clocks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these collapsed stellar cores, which are denser than white dwarfs.

tossups.p: J. Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff calculated in 1939 that these objects have a maximum possible mass, known as the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit. Above that limit, one of these objects collapses further into a black hole.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these remnants of massive stars, which can show up as pulsars.

tossups.p: Walter Baade [“BAH-duh”] and Fritz Zwicky [“TSVIK-ee”] predicted in 1933 that a supernova could turn an ordinary star into one of these objects, less than two years after the discovery of the particle these objects are mostly made of.
tossups.r: These objects are about the size of a city but hold more mass than the Sun. For 10 points, name these collapsed stars, often seen as pulsars.

tossups.p: These objects resist being crushed by their own gravity thanks to degeneracy pressure, which comes from the Pauli exclusion principle. A collapsing star core becomes one of these objects if it is above the Chandrasekhar [“chun-druh-SAY-kar”] limit, too heavy to become a white dwarf.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these city-sized stellar remnants that can spin hundreds of times per second.

tossups.p: In 1967, a graduate student noticed a strange radio signal that repeated every 1.3 seconds, which her team jokingly labeled LGM-1, for “Little Green Men.” That student, Jocelyn Bell, had found the first pulsar.
tossups.r: Pulsars turned out to be spinning examples of these objects. For 10 points, name these collapsed stars left behind by supernovae.

tossups.p: Antony Hewish shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for his role in discovering spinning examples of these objects, a decision that drew criticism because his student Jocelyn Bell, who first spotted the signal, was left out.
tossups.r: Spinning examples of these objects are called pulsars. For 10 points, name these extremely dense stellar remnants.

tossups.p: A type of these objects called magnetars has the strongest magnetic fields known in the universe, and starquakes on magnetars can blast out flashes of gamma rays. These objects are usually born spinning fast, because a shrinking star core conserves angular momentum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these super-dense objects, about the size of a city, that form when a massive star’s core collapses.

tossups.p: Many of these objects began as the iron cores of stars at least eight times as massive as the Sun. These objects are so dense that they are often compared to a single giant atomic nucleus, and their gravity bends light noticeably around them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these collapsed stars, smaller and denser than white dwarfs, that are sometimes seen as pulsars.

Incredibly dense: more mass than the Sun packed into a ball about 20 km (12 miles) across

A teaspoon of their material would weigh billions of tons

Hewish shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics, but Bell was left out, a decision that drew criticism

Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky predicted them in 1933, soon after James Chadwick discovered the particle they are mostly made of (1932)

They spin fast because a shrinking core conserves angular momentum, like a skater pulling in her arms

In 2017, LIGO and Virgo detected gravitational waves from two of them colliding (GW170817)

The first confirmed exoplanets (1992) orbit a pulsar; they were found by Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail

Pulsars sometimes suddenly spin faster, a “glitch” thought to come from a superfluid interior
Their crusts may hold “nuclear pasta,” matter squeezed into shapes nicknamed gnocchi, spaghetti, and lasagna
Scorpius X-1, the first X-ray source found beyond the solar system (1962), is one pulling gas from a companion star
