trap.title: Pulsar or the whole family?
trap.body: Pulsars and magnetars are kinds of neutron stars, so their clues fill neutron star tossups, and “Pulsars” is also an answer line of its own. Once a question has said that pulsars are spinning examples of “these objects,” answering “pulsar” is wrong. White dwarfs and black holes, the other two kinds of dead-star leftovers, are the other common mix-ups.
trap.fix: Think about how heavy the dead core is. A Sun-like star leaves an Earth-sized white dwarf, held up by electrons; a core above the Chandrasekhar limit makes a city-sized neutron star (Baade and Zwicky, Jocelyn Bell, the Crab pulsar); above the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit, it becomes a black hole. When in doubt, say “neutron star,” not “pulsar.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Neutron stars (accept neutron star; prompt on stars; do not accept “pulsars” or “magnetars”)

topics.name: Saturn
topics.kicker: Ringed sixth planet from the Sun · Less dense than water
topics.dates: Known since ancient times; rings first seen in 1610
topics.briefing: Saturn is the solar system’s ringed showpiece, but its rings are really countless chunks of ice, from dust grains to boulders, all orbiting together. The planet is so light for its size that it is less dense than water. Its biggest moon, Titan, has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane, and the Cassini spacecraft studied the whole system for 13 years before plunging into Saturn in 2017.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell showed that the rings of this planet could not be solid sheets or fluid, but must be made of countless separate particles. Most of those rings lie inside this planet’s Roche [“ROHSH”] limit, where tidal forces keep the particles from clumping into a moon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice.

tossups.p: Two shepherd moons, Prometheus and Pandora, keep this planet’s narrow F ring in shape, while the tiny moon Pan sweeps out a lane called the Encke [“EN-kee”] Gap. Giovanni Cassini discovered a wider gap between this planet’s A and B rings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, the second-largest in the solar system and the sixth from the Sun.

tossups.p: This planet’s rings were lettered in the order they were discovered, so starting from the planet they run D, C, B, A, F, G, and E. The faint outer E ring is fed by ice jets that spray from the moon Enceladus [“en-SEL-uh-dus”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, whose ring system is the largest and brightest in the solar system.

tossups.p: Giovanni Cassini noticed that this planet’s moon Iapetus [“eye-AP-ih-tus”] could be seen on only one side of this planet, because one half of that moon is dark and the other half is bright. Cassini also discovered a gap between this planet’s two brightest rings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ringed planet, the sixth from the Sun and the least dense planet.

tossups.p: William Pickering found this planet’s moon Phoebe [“FEE-bee”] in 1899, the first moon discovered in photographs. Phoebe orbits backward and sheds dust into an enormous, faint ring that was spotted in 2009 by the Spitzer Space Telescope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet whose largest moon, Titan, is wrapped in a thick, hazy atmosphere.

tossups.p: This planet’s moon Mimas [“MY-mus”] has a giant crater named Herschel that makes it look like the Death Star from _Star Wars_. Another of its moons, Enceladus, sprays jets of water ice from cracks called “tiger stripes.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sixth planet from the Sun, known for its spectacular rings.

tossups.p: In Voltaire’s story _Micromégas_, a giant from a planet circling the star Sirius travels to Earth with a companion from this planet. In Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_, this planet is called “the Bringer of Old Age.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, named for the Roman god who was the father of Jupiter.

tossups.p: When Galileo first viewed this planet in 1610, he thought it had two large companions, and two years later they seemed to vanish. They had not disappeared: this planet’s rings had simply turned edge-on to Earth, as they did again in 2009 and 2025.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sixth planet from the Sun, famous for its bright rings.

tossups.p: In 2005, a European probe parachuted through the orange haze of this planet’s largest moon, making what was, as of 2025, the most distant landing ever achieved. That moon has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
tossups.r: The probe was named for Christiaan Huygens, who discovered that moon, Titan. For 10 points, name this planet.

tossups.p: In 2017, the Cassini spacecraft made more than 20 dives through the gap between this planet and its innermost rings before plunging into this planet’s atmosphere. Cassini was crashed on purpose so it could never contaminate moons like Enceladus that might support life.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ringed planet that Cassini orbited for 13 years, starting in 2004.

tossups.p: A six-sided jet stream surrounds the north pole of this planet, a hexagon wider than Earth that the Voyager probes first photographed in the early 1980s. This planet spins in about 10 and a half hours, helping make it the most flattened planet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this planet, the least dense in the solar system, whose rings are its most famous feature.

tossups.p: In 2025, astronomers announced 128 newly found moons of this planet, widening its lead as the planet with the most known moons. Its biggest moon is the second-largest moon in the solar system and the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
tossups.r: That moon is Titan. For 10 points, name this ringed planet, the sixth from the Sun.

tossups.p: Pioneer 11 made the first flyby of this planet in 1979, followed by both Voyager probes. This planet is the only one less dense than water, so it would float in a big enough bathtub.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas giant, the sixth planet from the Sun, famous for its rings.

tossups.p: This planet’s astronomical symbol is shaped like the sickle of the god it is named for, who was linked to farming and the harvest. That god’s Greek counterpart swallowed his children to keep them from overthrowing him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ringed planet, named for the father of Jupiter.

tossups.p: Christiaan Huygens [“HOY-gunz”] first announced in a scrambled Latin anagram that this planet is circled by a thin, flat ring that touches it nowhere. In 1655, Huygens had discovered this planet’s largest moon.
tossups.r: That moon, Titan, has a thick nitrogen atmosphere. For 10 points, name this ringed planet, the second-largest in the solar system.

clues.t: Famous for its bright rings, made mostly of chunks of water ice
Sixth planet from the Sun and the second-largest planet
The least dense planet: less dense than water, so it would float in a big enough bathtub
Its largest moon, Titan, has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane
Named for the Roman god of farming, the father of Jupiter and counterpart of the Greek Cronus; its symbol looks like his sickle
Giovanni Cassini discovered the gap between its A and B rings, the Cassini Division, in 1675
NASA’s Cassini spacecraft orbited it from 2004 until it was crashed into the planet on purpose in 2017
Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan in 1655 and explained the rings as a thin, flat ring
Galileo saw it in 1610 but thought its rings were two companions on either side
Its moon Enceladus sprays jets of water ice from cracks called “tiger stripes,” feeding the E ring
A six-sided jet stream, the hexagon, swirls around its north pole
As of 2025, it had more known moons than any other planet, after 128 new ones were announced that year
Europe’s Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005, the most distant landing ever made as of 2025
Spins in about 10 and a half hours, helping make it the most flattened planet
James Clerk Maxwell showed that the rings must be made of countless separate particles, not solid sheets
Most of the rings lie inside its Roche limit, where tidal forces keep particles from clumping into a moon
Shepherd moons Prometheus and Pandora keep the narrow F ring in shape
The tiny moon Pan sweeps out the Encke Gap in the A ring
Its rings are lettered in order of discovery, so from the planet outward they run D, C, B, A, F, G, E
Its moon Iapetus is two-toned, one half dark and one half bright, as Giovanni Cassini, who discovered it in 1671, figured out
Its moon Mimas has a huge crater, Herschel, that makes it look like the Death Star from _Star Wars_
Its moon Phoebe orbits backward, was the first moon found in photographs (1899), and feeds a giant, faint ring
Cassini’s “Grand Finale” in 2017 took it through the gap between the planet and its rings more than 20 times
About every 15 years the rings turn edge-on to Earth and nearly vanish, as in 2009 and 2025
In Voltaire’s _Micromégas_, a giant from a planet circling the star Sirius travels with a companion from this planet
Gustav Holst’s _The Planets_ calls it “the Bringer of Old Age”
Huygens first announced his ring idea as a scrambled Latin anagram
Pioneer 11 made the first flyby, in 1979, followed by Voyager 1 and Voyager 2

trap.title: Not the only ringed planet
trap.body: All four giant planets have rings, so a ring clue alone does not prove the answer: Jupiter’s are faint and dusty, Uranus’s are thin and dark, and Neptune’s outermost ring is clumped into arcs. Saturn and Jupiter also share many clues, such as their hydrogen-and-helium makeup and huge storms. And when a question describes Titan or Enceladus, players sometimes answer with the moon instead of the planet.
trap.fix: Bright, wide, icy rings, the Cassini Division, the hexagon, Titan, Enceladus, Huygens, the Cassini mission, and “less dense than water” all mean Saturn. The Great Red Spot, the four Galilean moons, and Juno mean Jupiter. If the question says “this planet,” name the planet.

topics.name: Edwin Hubble
topics.kicker: Astronomer who found other galaxies · Showed the universe is expanding
topics.briefing: Edwin Hubble studied law at Oxford and taught high school before becoming the astronomer who made the universe bigger. Using the giant Hooker Telescope on Mount Wilson in California, he showed in the 1920s that the Andromeda “nebula” is a separate galaxy far beyond the Milky Way, and in 1929 that more distant galaxies are rushing away faster, evidence that the universe is expanding. The Hubble Space Telescope is named for him.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In October 1923, this astronomer crossed out the letter “N,” for nova, on a photographic plate of the Andromeda “nebula” and wrote “VAR!” because he had found a variable star. That star let him prove that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American astronomer, the namesake of a space telescope launched in 1990.

tossups.p: In 2018, the International Astronomical Union voted to recommend renaming a law named for this man so that it also honors Georges Lemaître [“luh-MET-ruh”], who had described the same idea in 1927. That law says galaxies recede from us at speeds proportional to their distances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American astronomer whose 1929 discovery showed that the universe is expanding.

tossups.p: Walter Baade [“BAH-duh”] showed in 1952 that there are two kinds of Cepheid variable stars, which meant that this astronomer’s distances to other galaxies were only about half as big as they should have been. This man’s first estimate of how fast the universe expands was about seven times too large.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who proved that the Andromeda Galaxy lies outside the Milky Way.

tossups.p: This scientist preferred the term “extragalactic nebulae” to the word “galaxies,” and he described his work in the 1936 book _The Realm of the Nebulae_. That book included his tuning-fork diagram, which sorts galaxies into ellipticals, spirals, and barred spirals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this astronomer who discovered that the universe is expanding.

tossups.p: This astronomer worked with Milton Humason [“HYOO-muh-sun”], a former mule driver who had hauled supplies up Mount Wilson while its observatory was being built, to measure the redshifts of faint galaxies. Together they showed that more distant galaxies are moving away faster.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American astronomer, the namesake of a famous space telescope.

tossups.p: This man was the first astronomer to observe with the giant 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory, in 1949. For most of his career, he had used the 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson, then the largest in the world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this astronomer who showed that the universe is expanding.

tossups.p: This man’s 1929 paper “A Relation between Distance and Radial Velocity among Extra-Galactic Nebulae” relied partly on redshifts that Vesto Slipher had measured years earlier. The paper showed that galaxies are moving away from us faster the farther away they are.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American astronomer who discovered the expansion of the universe.

tossups.p: This astronomer’s measurement of the distance to the Andromeda “nebula” settled the 1920 Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis, showing that Curtis was right that spiral nebulae are separate “island universes.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who used Cepheid variable stars to show that the Milky Way is only one of many galaxies.

tossups.p: Albert Einstein had added a cosmological constant to his equations to keep the universe static, but he dropped it after this astronomer’s discovery, and in 1931 Einstein visited Mount Wilson Observatory to meet him.
tossups.r: This man showed that galaxies are rushing away from one another. For 10 points, name this astronomer whose name is on a space telescope.

tossups.p: This man’s greatest discoveries depended on Henrietta Leavitt’s finding that Cepheid [“SEF-ee-id”] variable stars that pulse more slowly are brighter. Using that rule in the mid-1920s, he showed that the Andromeda “nebula” was hundreds of thousands of light-years away.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American astronomer who proved that other galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way.

tossups.p: Born in Marshfield, Missouri, this man worked as a lab assistant for Robert Millikan at the University of Chicago and then studied law at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar. He later taught high school Spanish and coached basketball in Indiana.
tossups.r: Returning to astronomy, he found that the universe is expanding. For 10 points, name this namesake of a space telescope.

tossups.p: After finishing his PhD research at Yerkes [“YUR-keez”] Observatory in 1917, this man served in the U.S. Army in World War I before taking a job at Mount Wilson. There, he proved that the Andromeda “nebula” is a separate galaxy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American astronomer who showed that the universe is expanding.

tossups.p: Dividing 1 by a constant named for this man gives a rough estimate of the age of the universe, but his own value for that constant made the universe seem younger than some rocks on Earth.
tossups.r: That constant measures how fast the universe expands. For 10 points, name this American astronomer.

tossups.p: In 1993, astronauts corrected a flaw in a space telescope whose main mirror had been ground to slightly the wrong shape. Two years later, that telescope’s Deep Field image showed thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky.
tossups.r: That telescope, launched in 1990, is named for this man. For 10 points, name this astronomer who proved that the Andromeda Galaxy lies far beyond the Milky Way.

tossups.p: In 1926, this man published a scheme for classifying galaxies by shape, labeling elliptical galaxies with the letter E and spirals with the letter S. The scheme’s diagram is drawn like a tuning fork, with ordinary and barred spirals on its two prongs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American astronomer, who also found that distant galaxies are rushing away from us.

clues.t: Showed in 1929 that the universe is expanding: more distant galaxies are moving away faster
The space telescope launched in 1990 aboard the space shuttle _Discovery_ is named for him
Proved that the Andromeda “nebula” is a separate galaxy far outside the Milky Way
American astronomer (1889–1953) who worked at Mount Wilson Observatory in California
A law named for him says a galaxy’s speed away from us is proportional to its distance
Measured the distance to Andromeda using Cepheid variable stars
His distances relied on Henrietta Leavitt’s rule that Cepheids that pulse more slowly are brighter
Used the 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson, then the largest telescope in the world
Sorted galaxies into ellipticals, spirals, and barred spirals on a diagram shaped like a tuning fork
Worked with Milton Humason, a former mule driver at Mount Wilson, to measure the redshifts of galaxies
His Andromeda result settled the 1920 Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis in Curtis’s favor
Albert Einstein dropped his idea of a static universe after this discovery and visited him at Mount Wilson in 1931
A Rhodes Scholar, he studied law at Oxford, then taught high school Spanish and coached basketball in Indiana
The telescope named for him took the 1995 Deep Field image, showing thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky
In October 1923, he crossed out an “N” (for nova) on a photographic plate of Andromeda and wrote “VAR!” for variable
In 2018, the International Astronomical Union voted to recommend renaming his law so it also honors Georges Lemaître, who described it in 1927
His first value for the universe’s expansion rate was about seven times too big
Walter Baade showed in 1952 that there are two kinds of Cepheids, which doubled his distances to galaxies
Wrote the 1936 book _The Realm of the Nebulae_
Preferred the term “extragalactic nebulae” to the word “galaxies”
His 1929 paper relied partly on redshifts measured years earlier by Vesto Slipher
Was the first astronomer to observe with the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory (1949)
Born in Marshfield, Missouri, in 1889; worked as a lab assistant for Robert Millikan at the University of Chicago
Finished his PhD research at Yerkes Observatory in 1917, then served in the U.S. Army in World War I
Dividing 1 by the constant named for him gives a rough age of the universe, but his value made the universe seem younger than some rocks on Earth
The space telescope named for him had a main mirror ground to the wrong shape, a flaw astronauts corrected in 1993
Published his galaxy classification scheme in 1926, labeling ellipticals E and spirals S

trap.title: The man, not the telescope
trap.body: Many things are named for Edwin Hubble: the Hubble Space Telescope, Hubble’s law, the Hubble constant, and the Hubble tuning fork. A question about the man may mention them as “named for this man,” and players who just heard about a telescope blurt out “Hubble Space Telescope,” which is wrong. Henrietta Leavitt (whose Cepheid rule he used), Georges Lemaître (who described the expansion law first), and Harlow Shapley (who argued that spiral nebulae lie inside the Milky Way) are the other wrong buzzes.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this man” or “this astronomer,” say “Hubble” or “Edwin Hubble” and nothing more. Clues about a telescope launched in 1990, its mirror, or its Deep Field image can appear, but the answer is still the person it was named for.

topics.name: Orion
topics.kicker: Constellation of the Hunter · Home of Betelgeuse, Rigel, and a famous belt
topics.dates: Known since ancient times; best seen on winter evenings
topics.briefing: Orion is the giant hunter of Greek myth, drawn in the sky with a belt of three bright stars in a row that almost anyone can find on a winter night. One shoulder holds Betelgeuse, a red supergiant so big that, in the Sun’s place, it would reach past the orbit of Mars. The fuzzy “star” in his sword is really the Orion Nebula, a cloud where new stars are being born.
topics.answerHtml: Orion (the constellation; do not accept “Orion Nebula” or “Orion’s Belt”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1920, Albert Michelson and Francis Pease used an interferometer at Mount Wilson to measure the angular size of a star in this constellation, the first star besides the Sun to have its size measured. That red supergiant would reach past the orbit of Mars if it replaced the Sun.
tossups.r: That star, Betelgeuse [“BEE-tul-jooz”], marks one of this figure’s shoulders. For 10 points, name this constellation of the hunter, which also contains Rigel.

tossups.p: In late 2019 and early 2020, the red supergiant at one shoulder of this constellation faded so much that skywatchers noticed, an event called the “Great Dimming.” Astronomers concluded that a cloud of dust thrown off by that star had blocked part of its light.
tossups.r: That star, Betelgeuse, may one day explode as a supernova. For 10 points, name this constellation whose belt is made of three bright stars in a row.

tossups.p: In 1880, Henry Draper took the first photograph ever made of a nebula, a glowing cloud in this constellation where new stars are forming. Four bright young stars called the Trapezium light up that cloud.
tossups.r: That cloud looks like the fuzzy middle “star” of this constellation’s sword. For 10 points, name this constellation that includes Betelgeuse and Rigel.

tossups.p: One star in this constellation, Mintaka, lies almost exactly on the celestial equator, so it rises due east and sets due west for people almost everywhere on Earth. Two other stars of this constellation, Alnilam and Alnitak, lie close to Mintaka in the sky.
tossups.r: Those three stars form its famous belt. For 10 points, name this constellation of a hunter from Greek myth.

tossups.p: In one myth, the earth goddess Gaia sent a giant scorpion to kill this constellation’s namesake after he boasted that he would slay every animal on Earth. Zeus is said to have placed the two enemies on opposite sides of the sky.
tossups.r: This constellation’s namesake was a great hunter. For 10 points, name this constellation whose brightest stars include Rigel and Betelgeuse.

tossups.p: After this constellation’s namesake was blinded by King Oenopion [“ee-NOH-pee-on”] of Chios, he regained his sight by traveling east to face the rising Sun. In Book 11 of the _Odyssey_, Odysseus sees his ghost in the underworld, still carrying a club of solid bronze.
tossups.r: This constellation’s brightest stars are Rigel and Betelgeuse. For 10 points, name this constellation of a great hunter from Greek myth.

tossups.p: The dark Horsehead Nebula is silhouetted against glowing gas just south of Alnitak, a star in this constellation. A huge, faint arc of glowing hydrogen called Barnard’s Loop curves around much of this constellation.
tossups.r: Its brightest stars are a blue supergiant called Rigel [“RYE-jul”] and a red supergiant called Betelgeuse. For 10 points, name this constellation shaped like a hunter.

tossups.p: Each October, Earth plows through dust left behind by Halley’s Comet, causing a meteor shower named for this constellation because its meteors seem to streak out of it. This constellation’s star Bellatrix, whose name is Latin for “female warrior,” marks one of its figure’s shoulders.
tossups.r: Its belt is three bright stars in a row. For 10 points, name this constellation of a hunter, home to Betelgeuse and Rigel.

tossups.p: Hubble Space Telescope images of a cloud in this constellation revealed many dusty disks around newborn stars, nicknamed “proplyds,” where planets may be forming. That cloud, about 1,300 light-years away, is the closest region to Earth where many massive stars are being born.
tossups.r: That cloud hangs from this constellation’s belt as part of its sword. For 10 points, name this constellation whose brightest stars are Rigel and Betelgeuse.

tossups.p: The Sun lies in a minor spiral arm of the Milky Way named for this constellation, since many of this constellation’s brightest stars lie in that arm too. In Spanish-speaking countries, three of this constellation’s stars are known as “Las Tres Marías,” or “the Three Marys.”
tossups.r: Its blue supergiant Rigel marks one of the figure’s feet. For 10 points, name this constellation of a hunter, which also contains Betelgeuse.

tossups.p: In one Greek myth, this constellation’s namesake chased the seven daughters of Atlas until Zeus placed them in the sky as the star cluster called the Pleiades [“PLEE-uh-deez”]. Ancient Egyptians linked this constellation to Sah, a god connected with Osiris.
tossups.r: This constellation faces Taurus, the bull. For 10 points, name this constellation of a mighty hunter, which includes Betelgeuse.

tossups.p: This constellation’s fairly faint star Meissa marks the head of its figure, which is often drawn holding a club and a shield. Canis Major and Canis Minor are said to be the dogs that follow this figure across the sky.
tossups.r: The three stars of its belt point toward Sirius, the brightest star at night. For 10 points, name this constellation of the hunter.

tossups.p: Skywatchers in Australia and New Zealand call part of this constellation “the Saucepan,” since from the Southern Hemisphere it appears upside down and its sword looks like the pan’s handle. Its stars Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka form the bottom of the pan.
tossups.r: Those three stars make up this constellation’s famous belt. For 10 points, name this constellation that contains Rigel and Betelgeuse.

tossups.p: Charles Messier gave the numbers 42 and 43 to two parts of a single glowing cloud in this constellation. On a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, this constellation’s two brightest stars sit near the top on opposite sides, one hot and blue and the other cool and red.
tossups.r: Those two supergiants are Rigel and Betelgeuse. For 10 points, name this constellation of a Greek hunter.

tossups.p: Some myths call this constellation’s namesake a son of Poseidon who could walk across the sea. In one story, Apollo tricked his sister Artemis into shooting at a far-off speck in the waves, which turned out to be this figure swimming.
tossups.r: The grieving goddess then placed him among the stars. For 10 points, name this constellation of a hunter, whose belt has three bright stars.

clues.t: Constellation named for a giant hunter in Greek mythology
Its famous belt is a short, straight row of three bright stars
Contains the bright stars Betelgeuse and Rigel
Easy to spot on winter evenings in the Northern Hemisphere
The fuzzy middle “star” of its sword is a star-forming nebula (Messier 42), about 1,300 light-years away
Betelgeuse, at one shoulder, is a red supergiant that may explode as a supernova someday
Rigel, at one foot, is a blue supergiant and usually its brightest star
In one myth, Gaia sent a giant scorpion to kill him, so he and Scorpius were placed on opposite sides of the sky
Some myths make him a son of Poseidon who could walk on the sea; Apollo tricked Artemis into shooting him by mistake
Canis Major and Canis Minor are said to be his hunting dogs
Its belt points one way to Sirius, the brightest star at night, and the other way to Aldebaran, the eye of Taurus the bull
Lies on the celestial equator, so it can be seen from almost everywhere on Earth
In myth he chased the seven daughters of Atlas until Zeus put them in the sky as the Pleiades
The dark Horsehead Nebula sits just south of its belt star Alnitak
In 1920, Michelson and Pease used an interferometer to measure Betelgeuse’s angular size, the first star besides the Sun to have its size measured
Betelgeuse’s “Great Dimming” (late 2019 to early 2020) was most likely caused by a cloud of dust it threw off
Henry Draper took the first photograph ever made of a nebula, the cloud in its sword, in 1880
Four bright young stars called the Trapezium light up the nebula in its sword
Hubble images of its great nebula revealed “proplyds,” dusty disks around newborn stars where planets may form
The belt stars are Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka; Mintaka lies almost exactly on the celestial equator
Bellatrix, Latin for “female warrior,” marks his other shoulder
The fairly faint star Meissa marks his head; he is often drawn with a club and a shield
An October meteor shower made of dust from Halley’s Comet is named for it
Barnard’s Loop, a huge faint arc of glowing hydrogen, curves around much of it
The Sun lies in a minor spiral arm of the Milky Way named for it
Australians call its upside-down belt and sword “the Saucepan”; in Spanish its belt stars are “the Three Marys”
Blinded by King Oenopion of Chios, he healed by facing the rising Sun; in the _Odyssey_ his ghost hunts in the underworld
Ancient Egyptians linked it to Sah, a god connected with Osiris

trap.title: Star, nebula, or constellation?
trap.body: Orion tossups are full of famous pieces of the constellation, and Betelgeuse, Rigel, and the Orion Nebula are all answer lines of their own. A player who recognizes the Great Dimming may blurt “Betelgeuse,” and one who hears about the Trapezium may say “Orion Nebula,” but when the question asks for “this constellation,” both are wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this star” wants Betelgeuse or Rigel, “this nebula” wants the Orion Nebula, and “this constellation” wants Orion. Don’t mix Orion up with Scorpius, the scorpion that killed him, or Canis Major, the dog that holds Sirius.

topics.name: Quasars
topics.kicker: Super-bright cores of distant galaxies · Powered by giant black holes
topics.briefing: A quasar is the blazing center of a faraway galaxy, where a supermassive black hole is feeding on gas so fast that the swirling disk around it can outshine all the galaxy’s stars combined. Astronomers first noticed them as radio sources that looked like ordinary stars, which is how they got their name, short for “quasi-stellar” (star-like) radio sources. Most are billions of light-years away, so we see them as they were when the universe was young.
topics.answerHtml: Quasars (accept quasar, quasi-stellar objects, QSOs, or quasi-stellar radio sources; prompt on active galactic nuclei or AGN)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1963, Maarten Schmidt realized that the strange lines in the spectrum of 3C 273 were ordinary hydrogen lines shifted toward the red by about 16 percent, showing that it lay far outside the Milky Way. Cyril Hazard had pinned down that radio source’s position by timing when the Moon passed in front of it.
tossups.r: 3C 273 was the first of these objects to have its redshift measured. For 10 points, name these super-bright cores of distant galaxies, powered by supermassive black holes.

tossups.p: The brightness of these objects can change in just days, which shows that the region giving off most of their light is only a few light-days across. In 1964, Hong-Yee Chiu coined the short name now used for these objects.
tossups.r: Their name comes from the fact that they first looked like faint stars. For 10 points, name these super-bright cores of distant galaxies.

tossups.p: In 1979, Dennis Walsh and his colleagues found two nearly identical images of one of these objects side by side, the first gravitational lens ever identified. Another of these objects, split into four images around a foreground galaxy, is called the Einstein Cross.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these blazing cores of faraway galaxies, each powered by a supermassive black hole.

tossups.p: Clouds of hydrogen gas lying between Earth and these objects leave a thicket of dark absorption lines in their spectra called the Lyman-alpha forest. In the most distant of these objects, one stretch of the spectrum is almost completely dark, a feature called the Gunn–Peterson trough.
tossups.r: These objects are so far away that we see them as they were billions of years ago. For 10 points, name these super-luminous centers of distant galaxies.

tossups.p: In 1960, Allan Sandage and Thomas Matthews matched the radio source 3C 48 with a faint point of light in a photograph, making it the first of these objects ever discovered. Its odd spectrum puzzled astronomers until a similar object’s lines were decoded three years later.
tossups.r: That decoded object, 3C 273, is the brightest of these objects in our sky. For 10 points, name these distant, star-like objects powered by supermassive black holes.

tossups.p: Some jets shot out by these objects seem to move faster than light, an illusion called superluminal motion that happens because the jets race toward us at nearly light speed. When one of these objects points its jet almost straight at Earth, astronomers call it a blazar.
tossups.r: These objects are powered by supermassive black holes. For 10 points, name these blazing centers of distant galaxies.

tossups.p: Because these objects are so far away that they never seem to move across the sky, the International Celestial Reference Frame uses many of them as fixed points for measuring positions. Radio astronomers who link telescopes on different continents also use them to measure the slow drift of those continents.
tossups.r: Each is powered by a supermassive black hole. For 10 points, name these extremely distant, luminous cores of galaxies.

tossups.p: These objects were strong evidence against the Steady State theory, because they are common at great distances but rare nearby, which means the universe has changed over time. Their numbers peaked when the universe was only a few billion years old.
tossups.r: Each one can outshine all the stars in its host galaxy. For 10 points, name these star-like objects powered by supermassive black holes.

tossups.p: The power of these objects comes from gas heated to enormous temperatures as it swirls in an accretion disk, a process that turns matter into energy far more efficiently than nuclear fusion does. Many of them shine hundreds of times brighter than the entire Milky Way.
tossups.r: That disk surrounds a supermassive black hole at a galaxy’s center. For 10 points, name these extremely bright, distant objects.

tossups.p: In 2007, Dutch schoolteacher Hanny van Arkel spotted a strange green cloud in telescope images while volunteering for Galaxy Zoo. That cloud, nicknamed Hanny’s Voorwerp [“VOHR-vairp”], was lit up by one of these objects in a neighboring galaxy, which has since faded.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these super-bright objects powered by supermassive black holes, first found as star-like radio sources.

tossups.p: Donald Lynden-Bell suggested in 1969 that burned-out examples of these objects lurk at the centers of many nearby galaxies, including the Milky Way. Seyfert [“SEE-fert”] galaxies have bright centers that resemble these objects but give off far less energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these super-luminous cores of distant galaxies, each powered by a supermassive black hole.

tossups.p: Although the first of these objects were found by radio telescopes, only about one in ten of them turned out to be a strong radio source. Many of the rest, called radio-quiet, were found by searching photographs for unusually blue points of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these super-bright cores of distant galaxies, whose name is short for “star-like radio source.”

tossups.p: By 2020, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey had cataloged hundreds of thousands of these objects by measuring their large redshifts. Light from the most distant ones left them when the universe was less than a billion years old.
tossups.r: Their huge redshifts show they are billions of light-years away. For 10 points, name these blazing centers of young galaxies, where supermassive black holes swallow gas.

tossups.p: Many of these objects shoot out narrow jets of particles at nearly the speed of light, feeding giant radio lobes far outside their galaxies. The brightest one in Earth’s sky, 3C 273, lies in the constellation Virgo, more than two billion light-years away.
tossups.r: They look like stars through a telescope. For 10 points, name these super-bright cores of distant galaxies, powered by supermassive black holes.

tossups.p: Several famous examples of these objects have names starting with “3C,” after the Third Cambridge Catalogue of Radio Sources. In 1971, one of them, 3C 279, became one of the first objects seen with jets that seem to move faster than light.
tossups.r: Through a telescope, they look like faint stars. For 10 points, name these super-bright objects powered by supermassive black holes.

clues.t: Powered by a supermassive black hole swallowing gas at the center of a galaxy
Their name means “star-like radio source,” because through a telescope they look like faint stars
Among the brightest objects in the universe: one can outshine all the stars in its host galaxy
Extremely distant: most are billions of light-years away, so we see them as they were long ago
In 1963, Maarten Schmidt found that the spectrum of 3C 273 showed hydrogen lines redshifted by about 16 percent
Their light comes from a super-hot accretion disk of gas, which turns matter into energy more efficiently than nuclear fusion
Huge redshifts in their spectra show how far away they are; by 2020 the Sloan Digital Sky Survey had cataloged hundreds of thousands
The brightest kind of active galactic nucleus (AGN)
Many shoot out narrow jets of particles at nearly light speed, feeding giant radio lobes
A blazar is one whose jet points almost straight at Earth
Common far away but rare nearby, they showed the universe changes over time, which was evidence against the Steady State theory
Their brightness can change within days, so their light comes from a region only light-days across
Hong-Yee Chiu coined their short name in 1964
Cyril Hazard pinned down the position of 3C 273 by timing when the Moon passed in front of it
3C 48, matched to a faint point of light by Allan Sandage and Thomas Matthews in 1960, was the first one discovered
3C 273, in the constellation Virgo, is the brightest one in Earth’s sky, more than two billion light-years away
Famous examples are named “3C” for the Third Cambridge Catalogue of Radio Sources
In 1979, Dennis Walsh’s team found a double image of one, the first gravitational lens ever identified
The Einstein Cross is one split into four images by a foreground galaxy
Hydrogen clouds between us and them leave a thicket of absorption lines called the Lyman-alpha forest
The most distant ones show a nearly dark stretch in their spectra called the Gunn–Peterson trough
Some of their jets, like those of 3C 279, seem to move faster than light, an illusion called superluminal motion
So far away that they never seem to move, they are fixed points in the International Celestial Reference Frame
Donald Lynden-Bell suggested in 1969 that burned-out ones lurk at the centers of nearby galaxies, including the Milky Way
Hanny’s Voorwerp, a green gas cloud spotted by a Galaxy Zoo volunteer in 2007, was lit up by one that has since faded
Only about one in ten is a strong radio source; the rest are called radio-quiet
Seyfert galaxies have bright centers like them but give off far less energy

trap.title: Quasar, pulsar, or AGN?
trap.body: Quasars and pulsars sound alike, but a pulsar is a spinning neutron star, usually inside our own galaxy, while a quasar is the brilliant core of a galaxy billions of light-years away. Blazars are close cousins of quasars whose jets point right at Earth, and “active galactic nucleus” (AGN) is the bigger family quasars belong to, so it earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for scale: steady radio pulses every second or so mean pulsar; huge redshifts, accretion disks, supermassive black holes, and 3C 273 mean quasar. If you get a prompt after saying “AGN,” narrow it down to “quasar.”
trap.line: Real answer line: quasars (accept quasi-stellar objects or QSOs; prompt on active galactic nuclei or AGN)

topics.name: Supernovae
topics.kicker: Exploding stars · Forge heavy elements and outshine whole galaxies
topics.dates: Earliest recorded 185 CE; named in the 1930s
topics.briefing: A supernova is the explosion of a star, so bright that for a few weeks one dying star can outshine its entire galaxy. Some happen when a giant star runs out of fuel and its core collapses; others happen when a white dwarf steals too much gas from a partner star and blows apart. These blasts scatter elements like oxygen and iron into space, so some of the atoms in your body were spread by exploding stars.
topics.answerHtml: Supernovae (accept supernova or supernovas; accept specific types such as Type Ia supernovae; prompt on stellar explosions; do not accept “nova”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On February 23, 1987, detectors in Japan and the United States caught a burst of neutrinos a few hours before the first light from one of these events in the Large Magellanic Cloud reached Earth. Masatoshi Koshiba shared a Nobel Prize partly for detecting those neutrinos.
tossups.r: That event, 1987A, was the closest of these explosions seen since 1604. For 10 points, name these explosions of stars, which can briefly outshine entire galaxies.

tossups.p: In 1998, two teams led by Saul Perlmutter and by Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess used distant examples of one type of these events to discover that the expansion of the universe is speeding up. That work won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
tossups.r: That type, called Ia, works as a “standard candle” because each blast peaks at nearly the same brightness. For 10 points, name these explosions of stars.

tossups.p: In 1572, Tycho Brahe saw a brilliant “new star” in Cassiopeia. By showing that it did not shift against the background stars the way the Moon does, he proved it lay far beyond the Moon, so the heavens could change after all.
tossups.r: He described it in his book _On the New Star_. For 10 points, name these powerful explosions of stars, which can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.

tossups.p: Chinese astronomers recorded a “guest star” in 1054 CE that was bright enough to see in daylight for 23 days. Some historians think a rock painting at Chaco Canyon in New Mexico also shows that event.
tossups.r: Its wreckage is the Crab Nebula, which has a spinning neutron star at its center. For 10 points, name these stellar explosions.

tossups.p: One kind of these events happens when a white dwarf pulls gas from a partner star until it nears about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, a cap called the Chandrasekhar [“chun-druh-SAY-kar”] limit. The white dwarf then blows itself apart in a runaway burst of carbon fusion.
tossups.r: That kind is called Type Ia. For 10 points, name these huge stellar explosions, which can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.

tossups.p: Inside very massive stars, fusion builds up a core of iron, which cannot release energy by fusing further. Once that core grows too heavy, it collapses in less than a second, and a flood of neutrinos carries away most of the energy.
tossups.r: The rebound blasts the star’s outer layers into space, leaving a neutron star or black hole behind. For 10 points, name these stellar explosions.

tossups.p: Walter Baade [“BAH-duh”] and Fritz Zwicky [“TSVIK-ee”] coined the name for these events in the early 1930s and suggested that they produce cosmic rays. Zwicky later found more than a hundred of them by searching photographs of other galaxies.
tossups.r: Baade and Zwicky also predicted that these blasts leave behind neutron stars. For 10 points, name these explosions of stars, which can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.

tossups.p: A famous 1957 paper by Margaret and Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler, and Fred Hoyle explained how stars forge chemical elements, including in these events. Some elements heavier than iron may be built in these events by rapid neutron capture, called the r-process.
tossups.r: Much of the iron in your blood was spread through space by these blasts. For 10 points, name these explosions of stars.

tossups.p: Astronomers in Egypt, China, and Japan recorded one of these events in 1006 CE in the constellation Lupus, the brightest stellar event in recorded history. The Egyptian astronomer Ali ibn Ridwan left one of the best descriptions of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these explosions of stars, which can briefly shine brighter than a whole galaxy.

tossups.p: Mark Phillips showed in 1993 that the brighter examples of one kind of these events fade more slowly, which lets astronomers correct their brightness and measure distances. Other examples of these events stay bright on a long “plateau” in their light curves for about a hundred days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these stellar explosions, whose Type Ia kind helps measure distances across the universe.

tossups.p: Cassiopeia A, one of the brightest radio sources in the sky, is the expanding wreckage of one of these events whose light reached Earth around 1680, although almost no one noticed it. In 1999, the Chandra X-ray Observatory’s first image revealed a tiny hot object at its center.
tossups.r: That object is a neutron star. For 10 points, name these stellar explosions, which also left behind the Crab Nebula.

tossups.p: Some extremely massive stars may end in a rare “pair-instability” version of these events, in which gamma rays inside the star turn into pairs of electrons and positrons. Such a blast would leave no neutron star or black hole behind.
tossups.r: The red supergiant Betelgeuse is expected to end its life in one of these events. For 10 points, name these blasts that end the lives of many massive stars.

tossups.p: The earliest written record of one of these events comes from Chinese astronomers in 185 CE, who described a “guest star” that stayed visible for months. Its leftover shell of gas is thought to be RCW 86.
tossups.r: Such blasts can briefly outshine a whole galaxy of stars. For 10 points, name these stellar explosions, some of which leave behind neutron stars.

tossups.p: The glow of many of these events fades slowly for months because it is powered by the radioactive decay of nickel-56 into cobalt-56 and then iron. Astronomers sort these events into types by whether their spectra show hydrogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these stellar explosions, whose Type Ia kind happens when a white dwarf blows apart.

tossups.p: Galileo gave public lectures in Padua about one of these events that appeared in 1604 in the constellation Ophiuchus, arguing that it lay far beyond the Moon. Johannes Kepler wrote a book about that same event, which is now named for him.
tossups.r: It was the last of these blasts seen in the Milky Way without a telescope. For 10 points, name these stellar explosions.

clues.t: A gigantic explosion of a star that can briefly outshine its whole galaxy
Ends the lives of many stars that are much more massive than the Sun
Can leave behind a neutron star or a black hole
The Crab Nebula is the wreckage of one that Chinese astronomers saw in 1054 CE
Betelgeuse, a red supergiant in Orion, is expected to explode as one someday
Type Ia: a white dwarf pulls gas from a partner star and blows itself apart
The white dwarf explodes as it nears the Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass
Type Ia ones peak at nearly the same brightness, so they work as “standard candles” for measuring distances
In 1998, Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt, and Adam Riess used them to find that the universe’s expansion is speeding up (2011 Nobel Prize)
Core-collapse ones happen when a massive star’s iron core, which can’t fuse any further, collapses in under a second
Type II spectra show hydrogen lines; Type I spectra do not
1987A, in the Large Magellanic Cloud, was the closest seen since 1604; its neutrinos arrived hours before its light
Tycho Brahe’s 1572 one in Cassiopeia proved the heavens can change; he wrote _On the New Star_
Kepler’s 1604 one, in Ophiuchus, was the last one seen in the Milky Way without a telescope
They scatter elements like oxygen and iron into space, where they end up in new stars and planets
Masatoshi Koshiba shared the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics partly for detecting the neutrinos from 1987A
Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky named them in the early 1930s and linked them to cosmic rays and neutron stars; Zwicky later found more than a hundred
A 1957 paper by the Burbidges, William Fowler, and Fred Hoyle explained how stars and these blasts forge elements
Some elements heavier than iron may be built in them by rapid neutron capture, the r-process
The one seen in 1006 CE in Lupus was the brightest stellar event in recorded history; Ali ibn Ridwan described it
The earliest recorded one was a Chinese “guest star” in 185 CE; its leftover shell is thought to be RCW 86
The 1054 one was visible in daylight for 23 days; some historians think a Chaco Canyon rock painting shows it
Mark Phillips (1993): brighter Type Ia ones fade more slowly, which lets astronomers correct their brightness
Some core-collapse ones stay bright on a “plateau” in their light curves for about a hundred days
Their slowly fading glow is powered by radioactive nickel-56 decaying into cobalt-56 and then iron
Cassiopeia A, a bright radio source, is the wreckage of one whose light reached Earth around 1680; Chandra’s first image (1999) found a neutron star inside
Some extremely massive stars may die in “pair-instability” blasts, where gamma rays turn into electron–positron pairs, leaving nothing behind
Galileo lectured in Padua on the 1604 one, arguing that it lay far beyond the Moon

trap.title: Nova, supernova, or remnant?
trap.body: A nova is a much smaller outburst on the surface of a white dwarf that survives, so “nova” is wrong for a star that blows apart. The Crab Nebula and Cassiopeia A are the wreckage left behind, and neutron stars and black holes are what a collapsed core becomes; each is a different answer line. Players who hear “white dwarf” in a Type Ia clue sometimes buzz with “white dwarf,” but the question wants the explosion.
trap.fix: Ask what the question’s noun is: “these explosions” or “these events” means supernovae; “this nebula” means a remnant like the Crab; “these objects” left behind means neutron stars or black holes. You can name the type (“Type Ia supernova”) when the clues focus on white dwarfs, but plain “supernova” is the safe answer for general questions.
trap.line: Real answer line: supernovae (accept supernovas; accept specific types)

topics.name: Pluto
topics.kicker: Dwarf planet beyond Neptune · Called the ninth planet until 2006
topics.dates: Discovered 1930; reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006
topics.briefing: In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh, a 24-year-old who had grown up on a Kansas farm, found Pluto by flipping back and forth between photographs of the night sky, and an 11-year-old English girl suggested its name. For 76 years it was called the ninth planet, until astronomers reclassified it as a dwarf planet in 2006. When NASA’s New Horizons probe flew past in 2015, it found a giant heart-shaped region, half of it a plain of frozen nitrogen.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old schoolgirl in Oxford, England, suggested this world’s name to her grandfather, who passed it on to astronomers. Its name’s first two letters also honor Percival Lowell, who had searched for a “Planet X” beyond Neptune.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, named for the Roman god of the underworld.

tossups.p: This object was found by using a blink comparator to flip back and forth between two photographs of the same patch of sky, taken six days apart. Some of its discoverer’s ashes later flew past this world aboard a NASA probe.
tossups.r: That discoverer, Clyde Tombaugh, found it at Lowell Observatory in 1930. For 10 points, name this world, called the ninth planet until 2006.

tossups.p: This world fails the test of having “cleared the neighborhood” around its orbit, because it shares its region of space with many other icy bodies. The 2005 discovery of the more massive Eris pushed astronomers to write that rule at a meeting in Prague.
tossups.r: In 2006, this world was reclassified as a dwarf planet. For 10 points, name this world, once called the ninth planet.

tossups.p: Sputnik Planitia, a vast basin of nitrogen ice on this world, slowly churns in giant cells, like a lava lamp. That basin forms the western half of a bright region named for this world’s discoverer.
tossups.r: That region, Tombaugh Regio, is shaped like a heart. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet that New Horizons flew past in 2015.

tossups.p: This world and its largest moon always keep the same faces toward each other, and the point they orbit lies in the empty space between them, so some astronomers call them a double system. That moon, about half this world’s width, was discovered by James Christy in 1978.
tossups.r: That moon is Charon. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, once called the ninth planet.

tossups.p: This world circles the Sun twice for every three orbits of Neptune, a resonance that keeps the two from ever coming close to each other even though their orbits seem to cross. From 1979 to 1999, this world was closer to the Sun than Neptune was.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, which takes about 248 years to orbit the Sun.

tossups.p: In 2005, the Hubble Space Telescope found two small moons of this world, Nix and Hydra, and later images revealed two more, Kerberos and Styx. Nix was spelled with an “i” so it would not be confused with an asteroid named Nyx.
tossups.r: This world’s largest moon is Charon. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, named for the Roman god of the underworld.

tossups.p: After passing this world, a NASA probe went on to fly past the small, snowman-shaped Kuiper Belt object Arrokoth on New Year’s Day 2019. That probe, launched in January 2006, took about nine and a half years to reach this world.
tossups.r: That probe, New Horizons, flew past this world on July 14, 2015. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet whose largest moon is Charon.

tossups.p: Methane gas escaping from this world freezes onto the north pole of its largest moon, where ultraviolet light turns it into reddish chemicals called tholins, staining a region nicknamed Mordor Macula. Spacecraft images showed that this world’s thin nitrogen atmosphere holds layers of blue haze.
tossups.r: That moon is Charon. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930.

tossups.p: This world’s Tenzing Montes and Hillary Montes, mountain ranges named for the first two people to climb Mount Everest, are made of water ice that is as hard as rock in the extreme cold. Some scientists think an ocean of liquid water may lie deep beneath its icy surface.
tossups.r: Its largest moon is Charon. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, which was called the ninth planet for 76 years.

tossups.p: Glenn Seaborg’s team named element 94 for this world, just as the two elements before it had been named for Uranus and Neptune. Heat from that radioactive element powers the spacecraft that NASA sent to visit this world.
tossups.r: It was discovered in 1930. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, named for the Roman god of the underworld.

tossups.p: This world’s orbit is tilted about 17 degrees from the plane of the planets and is so stretched out that its distance from the Sun ranges from about 30 to 49 times Earth’s. It last passed its closest point to the Sun in 1989.
tossups.r: It lies in the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet, once called the ninth planet.

tossups.p: This world is smaller than seven moons in the solar system, including Earth’s Moon and Neptune’s moon Triton, which may have formed in the same region of space. Its surface is mostly frozen nitrogen, with some methane and carbon monoxide ice.
tossups.r: Its biggest moon is Charon. For 10 points, name this dwarf planet that Clyde Tombaugh discovered in 1930.

tossups.p: The discovery of this world was announced on March 13, which would have been Percival Lowell’s 75th birthday and was also the anniversary of William Herschel’s discovery of Uranus. Lowell had spent his last years hunting for an unseen planet beyond Neptune.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this world found by Clyde Tombaugh, which was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

tossups.p: The American Dialect Society once chose as its Word of the Year a verb based on this world’s name, meaning “to demote or devalue someone or something.” This world’s thin atmosphere may partly freeze onto its surface as it moves farther from the Sun.
tossups.r: In 2006, this world lost its planet status and became a dwarf planet. For 10 points, name this icy world beyond Neptune.

trap.title: Pluto, Charon, or Hades?
trap.body: Many Pluto tossups lead with clues about its moon Charon or about Kuiper Belt neighbors like Eris and Arrokoth, and players who recognize those names blurt them out. Mythology fans sometimes say “Hades,” the Greek god, but the dwarf planet uses only the Roman name. Eris is a special trap: its discovery set off the 2006 vote, but when the question says “this world” was reclassified, it wants Pluto.
trap.fix: “This dwarf planet” plus Clyde Tombaugh, Venetia Burney, Charon, the heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio, or New Horizons in 2015 means Pluto. Eris was found in 2005 and has a moon named Dysnomia; Ceres is the dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.
